To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) children learn vocabulary and spelling by reading, and (2) the amount of reading they do is the main factor in determining how much they learn.

(a) the vocabulary and spelling of second language learners are not acquired by formal instruction, but rather by reading, and (b) the vocabulary and reading of first language learners are not learned by formal instruction, either, but rather by listening to and reading books and stories.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the acquisition of English spelling and vocabulary, and the relationship between these two areas of language.
the acquisition of vocabulary, spelling, reading, and writing.

vocabulary is the most important aspect of language learning, as it is the foundation of all language.
reading is the most effective way of acquiring vocabulary and spelling skills.
the acquisition of vocabulary is the process of learning words and the meanings of the words in a language.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the input hypothesis is supported by the evidence of vocabulary and spelling.
the input hypothesis is a good hypothesis, but not as good as the interaction hypothesis, and that the interaction hypothesis is a good explanation of how we acquire language.
the input hypothesis is a powerful explanation of the acquisition process and that the input hypothesis can account for many of the facts of language acquisition.

we need to pay more attention to the vocabulary of our students, not less.
vocabulary and spellings are acquired through exposure to print and not through explicit instruction, and this is true for all ages and all levels of ability.
